item.research_question: How local chemistry affects enhanced deformation mechanisms and the origin of strain hardening in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.
item.material_system: Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 high-entropy alloy (at.%) comprising face-centered cubic (fcc) austenite and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) ε-martensite phases.
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction casting of 4-kg ingots, hot rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h with water quenching, cold rolling to 40–50% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1); in situ TEM straining at ambient temperature (200 kV, loading rate ~1 μm/s); nanoscale pillar compression (300 nm diameter, 2 nm/s displacement rate).
key_findings: The alloy exhibits a tensile strength approaching 1 GPa and ductility of almost 60% at ambient temperatures.
Partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks comprising multiple stacking faults and sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks.
The fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase.
Dual-phase pillars displayed the highest ultimate strength at ~3.45 GPa, compared to ~2.25 GPa for pure hcp and ~1.25 GPa for pure fcc pillars.
Local chemical composition variations show Ni atomic fraction fluctuating from −58% to 115% about its average, with Mn near stacking faults being nearly 30% higher than in the matrix.
The continuous fcc → hcp phase transformation sustains a hardening effect where flow stress increases two-fold from 1.75 to ~3.5 GPa.
Lomer–Cottrell locks act to immobilize dislocation motion and provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of stable 3D stacking-fault networks. These networks impede dislocation motion (work hardening) and serve as preferred sites for the nucleation and growth of the hcp phase via a transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, where the continuous increase in the hcp volume fraction drives the ultrahigh strain hardening.
item.limitations: The fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures, because the product hcp ε-martensite phase tends to be quite brittle.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the intentional generation of Lomer–Cottrell locks raises a fundamental question of how to increase the probability of interactions between dissociated dislocations with the sole objective of enhancing the formation of such locks.
quotes: variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of the stacking-fault networks to provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation.

the fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase, serving as the major source of strain hardening.
